title: A Storm Sucked Her Higher Than Everest. She Blacked Out, and Woke Up Still Flying
description:
Case 006, the full case file. On 14 February 2007, ten days before the Paragliding World Championships at Manilla, New South Wales, more than a hundred pilots flew a warm-up task from Mount Borah. Ewa Wiśnierska, 35, born in Poland and flying for Germany, the 2005 World Cup winner, launched around noon in sunshine; the forecast warned that thunderstorms were possible later. About two hours into the flight two clouds ahead of her grew and joined. She tried to fly around the storm, then tried repeatedly to spiral down against its lift, and was pulled up at about 20 metres a second. She radioed her team leader that it was raining and hailing and that she was still climbing. In about fifteen minutes she was carried to almost 10,000 metres, higher than Everest, into hail, lightning, temperatures around 40 below zero and air too thin to stay conscious. She was out for more than half an hour while the glider flew on by itself. She came round with frozen gloves and iced-up brake handles, scratched the ice off her GPS, found she was still almost 7,000 metres up, and spiralled down to land beside a farm about 60 kilometres from the launch, roughly three and a half hours after take-off. Her team reached her by mobile phone and drove out to her. She was treated for frostbite to her ears and face and bruises from the hail, and left hospital after about an hour. Doctors said losing consciousness may have saved her, because her body then needed less oxygen. The event's organiser compared her odds to winning the lottery ten times in a row. She kept flying, had the figure 9946 stitched onto her glider, and now teaches paragliding in Bavaria. The 2010 documentary Miracle in the Storm retells the flight. Rook didn't believe it either.

In memory of He Zhongpin, 42, a member of the Chinese paragliding team with more than ten years of flying, who died in the same storm.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. Scenes, sets and all of Rook's actions are dramatised; nobody's words are quoted.
title_options: A Storm Sucked Her Higher Than Everest. She Blacked Out, and Woke Up Still Flying
Sucked Up to Almost 10,000 Metres by a Thunderstorm: The Full Case of Ewa Wiśnierska
She Spiralled Down Three Times. The Storm Took Her Up Past Everest Anyway
Out Cold for Half an Hour Under a Paraglider, 10 km Up. Then Her Phone Rang
The Paraglider a Thunderstorm Swallowed: What Really Happened Over Manilla in 2007
source_notes: LONG-FORM ADDITIONS (checked on 14 Nov 2026). How it was checked: the pages were opened in full for this run: the AP report (Rod McGuirk, as carried by The Spokesman-Review, 17 Feb 2007), Wikipedia, Women's Adventure Magazine ('In the Eye of the Storm', Tom LeCompte, 7 Mar 2008, a long interview feature; 'WAM' below), People magazine's first-person interview as carried by AOL (Johnny Dodd; 'People'), the Reuters post-mortem report carried by The Star (20 Feb 2007), ABC News / Good Morning America (Ned Potter, 16-17 Feb 2007) and the ABC World News transcript on AviationPros, Dawn (agencies, 17 Feb 2007), the Cloud Appreciation Society (26 Apr 2007), Cross Country magazine (29 May 2025, one paragraph) and the free part of a Noiser podcast page (dramatised and promotional, so it is only ever used as a second source). NBC (robots refusal), abcnews.go.com (redirect not followed) and China Daily (error) could not be opened and are not used. Who: 35 (AP, Dawn); 'Polish-born German' (Dawn); born in Nysa, Poland, member of the German national team (Wikipedia); 'born and raised in Poland' (WAM); 'Paragliding 2005 World Cup winner' (AP), 'in 2005 winning the Female World Cup' (WAM). The script says 'two years earlier she won the Paragliding World Cup'. Why there: a warm-up/training cross-country task before the 2007 World Championships at Manilla (WAM, People, AP); the championships began on Saturday 24 February (Reuters: 'begin on Saturday'; Wikipedia), ten days after 14 February. Pilots flying that day: 'most of the 120 or so pilots' (WAM), '200 other competitors' (People); the script says 'more than a hundred' and the graphic 100+ PILOTS. Launch: Mount Borah 'at around noon', 'sunny, with small clouds' (WAM); 'just before midday ... from Mount Borah' (Noiser). Forecast: 'isolated showers and thunderstorms' (WAM, quoting organiser Godfrey Wenness), 'in the afternoon there's a possibility of thunderstorms' (People); Wikipedia words it more strongly ('in spite of a forecast of violent thunderstorms') and Dawn says both pilots 'ignored advice'; the script keeps to the two interview sources and passes no judgement. Flight north: wind from the south, pilots went north (WAM, People); after about two hours two clouds grew together / merged (WAM, People; Wikipedia-derived pages: 'two joining thunderstorms'). Escape attempts: tried to skirt the storm, then 'repeatedly attempted to spiral against its powerful lift' (AP); three spiral attempts (WAM); the script's 'Once. Twice. Three times.' follows WAM. 'Cloud suck' is the pilots' term (Cross Country). Climb rate: 'up to 21 m/s' (Wikipedia, GPS variometer), 20 m/s (Cloud Appreciation Society), 4,000 ft/min (WAM), '24 yards per second' (People); normal lift 'about 4 yards per second' (People), 'three or four metres per second' (Noiser). The script says 'about twenty' and 'three or four'. Radio: 'She radioed her team leader at 13,123 feet ... It's raining and hailing, and I'm still climbing' (AP); People has the call at 5,000 m with the same content. The script reports the content indirectly and gives no height; the flight-computer insert in that scene shows digits running between 3,600 and 5,200 m without settling. The team leader is not named in any source read and is a generic figure. Inside the cloud: darkness, hail, lightning 'in front of me, behind me, around me' (Dawn; ABC). Top: 'from 2,500 feet to her maximum height in about 15 minutes' (AP, Wenness); maximum 9,946 m (WAM, Cross Country, Wikipedia-derived pages) or 32,612 ft = 9,940 m (AP) or 10,054 m (Wikipedia from GPS data), so the script says 'nearly ten thousand metres'. Temperature: about -40 (WAM gives -40 F, which is also -40 C; Cloud Appreciation Society -40 to -50 C; Noiser -40 C; People 'probably around minus 55'); the script says 'around forty below zero'. Blackout: more than 30 minutes (AP), 30 to 40 (WAM), about 40 (Dawn, Cross Country), about 45 (People), 'almost an hour' (Reuters, ABC); the script says 'more than half an hour'. Glider 'flew on uncontrolled, sinking and lifting several times' (AP). Doctors: 'passing out may have saved her. Her body needed less oxygen' (ABC narration; Dr Ken Harrison of the rescue service called it 'a kind of medical miracle'); WAM adds that hypothermia would have slowed her metabolism. The oxygen-bar graphic is an illustration with no measured values. Waking: she thought only a moment had passed; her gloves were frozen and the brakes 'covered in ice'; she scratched ice off her GPS (WAM, People). Height on waking: GPS 6,900 m (WAM), 'around 22,966 feet' = 7,000 m (People). The first AP and ABC reports said she regained consciousness at about 1,640 / 1,500 ft; the script follows her own two later accounts ('still almost seven thousand metres up') and the GPS insert shows '6,9' with the last digits iced over. Descent and landing: the glider was open and flying; she spiralled down (WAM, People); landed beside a farm (WAM: pastures and a fence; People: farmland, she saw cows), 'about 60 kilometres north of her starting position' (Wikipedia) after about three and a half hours (People; Wikipedia 'more than three hours'). People's introduction says 54 miles; the script says 'roughly sixty kilometres'. Found: her radio was dead; her mobile rang, it was her team; she sent GPS coordinates and they reached her (People: about 45 minutes later; WAM: 'in a short time'). Injuries: frostbite to face and ears (Reuters: 'severe frost bite and blistering to her face and ears'; WAM: nose and ears; AP: face), bruises from hail (WAM; ABC 'a few bruises and mild frostbite'); 'stayed only an hour in the hospital' (ABC; AP). Odds: 'It's like winning Lotto 10 times in a row' (Godfrey Wenness, event organiser, AP only); reported indirectly. He Zhongpin: 42, 'a member of the Chinese paragliding team with more than 10 years experience', body 'found the next day 75 km from where he had taken off', preliminary post-mortem: 'struck by lightning' (Reuters); WAM and Wikipedia also say lightning. AP's first report (before the post-mortem) said 'apparently from a lack of oxygen and extreme cold'. The script follows the post-mortem. He is not depicted: the film shows the empty hill at dusk, the storm moving away, two plain cards and Rook lowering his hat. Afterwards: 'Ewa continues to fly and compete' and had 9946 stitched into her glider (WAM, 2008; the stitched number is in that one source only); she now flies for pleasure and runs a paragliding school (People), lives in Aschau im Chiemgau, Bavaria, 'where she teaches paragliding' (Wikipedia). Documentary: Miracle in the Storm, 2010, ABC1 and France 5 (Wikipedia; People calls it a '2010 Australian documentary'). Whether she flew in the 2007 championships was not confirmed (Reuters only says she hoped to), so it is not mentioned. Dramatised in the long form, not reported: the look of every new set (briefing shed and weather board, launch queue, the plains from the air, the dirt road and the team's ute, the hospital room, the alpine meadow and chalet), the crowd of pilots, the two cloud towers as drawn, the radio on her shoulder strap, the team leader's appearance, the GPS unit, the cows, the phone, the pick-up, the doctor and his clipboard, the dressings, the lottery tickets, the stitching of the number, the students, and everything Rook does. The 'cloud suck: the storm breathes in' line is a figure of speech. No dialogue is attributed to anyone; on-screen words are labels. Pronunciations ('Eva Vishnyairska', 'Huh Jong-pin') were not checked by ear. FROM THE SHORT: Read for this run: two Associated Press reports (Rod McGuirk, Canberra, 16-17 Feb 2007, as carried by The Spokesman-Review and Fox News), Dawn (agencies, 17 Feb 2007), AVweb (18 Feb 2007) and Wikipedia. NBC and ABC News pages could not be opened by this run and are not used. Date and place: 14 February 2007 near Manilla, New South Wales; she was training for the 2007 World Paragliding Championships, which began on 24 February (Wikipedia, AP). Who: Ewa Wisnierska, 35, 'German champion' and 'Paragliding 2005 World Cup winner' (AP); 'Polish-born German' (Dawn); member of the German national team (Wikipedia). The script says 'German pilot'; the description adds that she was born in Poland. Escape attempts: she 'attempted to skirt the thunderstorm and when that failed, repeatedly attempted to spiral against its powerful lift' (AP). Climb: organiser Godfrey Wenness said she went 'from 2,500 feet to her maximum height in about 15 minutes' (AP); AVweb says about 10 minutes; the script says 'about fifteen minutes'. Height: 32,612 ft, about 9,940 m (AP, from her GPS and radio equipment); 'about 30,000 feet' (Dawn, AVweb); Wikipedia's lead says 'almost 10,000 metres' and its body 10,054 m from GPS data. Because the figures differ, the script says 'nearly ten kilometres' and 'higher than Everest' (AP headline; Everest is 8,849 m), the graphics say ALMOST 10 KM / ALMOST 10,000 m, and the flight-computer insert shows digits racing upward that never settle on an exact figure. Conditions: hail and lightning in her own words ('It's raining and hailing and I'm still climbing', AP; 'I could hear lightning in front of me, behind me, around me', Dawn); 'lack of oxygen' and extreme cold (AP, Wikipedia). The -50 C figure and 'orange-sized hail' appear only in AVweb and are not used. Blackout: 'more than 30 minutes while her paraglider flew on uncontrolled, sinking and lifting several times' (AP); about 40 minutes (Dawn); about an hour (AVweb). The script says 'over half an hour' and the stopwatch insert stops at 30+ MIN. Waking: AP says she regained consciousness at about 1,640 ft, AVweb after a descent to about 20,000 ft; the sources disagree, so no height is given for it. Ice: she landed 'covered in ice' (Dawn), 'coated in ice' (AVweb), with 'ice in her lightweight flying suit' (AP). Landing: she 'landed safely' (AP); Wikipedia says more than three hours after launch and about 60 km north of her starting point (not used). Injuries: frostbite to her face, an hour in hospital for observation (AP); frostbite and bruises (AVweb). The script says 'She walks away with frostbite.' He Zhongpin: 42, from China, died in the same weather system; AP reported the cause as apparently lack of oxygen and extreme cold, Wikipedia says a lightning strike, so the script says only that the same storm killed him; his body was found the next day about 75 km from his launch site (AP; not shown). He is not depicted; the film shows an empty launch hill at dusk, a plain memorial card and Rook lowering his hat. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the launch hill, the plains, the windsock, the paddock, the windmill and water tank; the colours of her wing, suit and helmet; the flight computer and climb gauge (the gauge shows no number); the exact moment and manner of her blackout and waking; the hand on the brake handle; her landing on her knees; her wave in the paddock; the pilot-file card layout; and everything Rook does (the umbrella, the icicle). No dialogue is attributed to anyone. Pronunciation: 'Ewa Wisnierska' is spelled 'Eva Vishnyairska' and 'He Zhongpin' 'Huh Jong-pin' for the synthetic voice; neither was checked by ear.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet (16:9) reviewed in two rounds with fixes after each (staging, camera angles, re-framed repeats, the hospital room's exposure, the thumbnail), composited stills (inserts, overlays, captions, HUD) in a third round with layout fixes, then a full-length low-resolution rehearsal (384x216, 4 samples) composited with sound and reviewed at one frame every 1.07 s, and a second pass after re-rendering the four changed shots. The 1280x720 thumbnail was restaged twice so the hook sits inside the frame and off the subjects. The rehearsal passed the automated gate locally: 87 shots, mean 1.99 s, longest 2.85 s, loudness -15.0 LUFS, true peak -1.5 dBFS, voice 13.3 dB over the bed, host in 37/87 shots (43%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.77; the quietest 3.5 s window without a detected cut has a mean frame change of 1.80 against the 0.8 minimum. Audio was measured, not listened to. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud.
